newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela's Cerro Negro oil to cost $2.10/barrel.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela's Cerro Negro oil to cost $2.10/barrel.

text.p: The operating costs of Venezuela's Cerro Negro heavy oil venture will total $2.10 for each barrel of upgraded crude oil produced, according to an official document outlining the project.

The $2.5 billion project, which joins state oil subsidiary Lagoven (41.67 percent) with Mobil (41.67 percent) and Veba (16.67 percent), is currently being discussed in Congress which has to approve all foreign participation in Venezuela's nationalised oil industry.

The Cerro Negro venture is one of at least six such schemes to exploit the massive heavy oil reserves in Venezuela's Orinoco Oil Belt. The project includes production facilities in Cerro Negro, a crude oil pipeline to Jose on the north coast of Venezuela and a deep conversion plant in Jose.
The project document says Cerro Negro contains 2 billion barrel of recoverable oil reserves, with a recovery rate of 10- 12.5 percent.
The participants are hoping to make use of several tax concessions and royalty discounts which should give the project a real internal rate of return of 20 percent.

Cerro Negro's operating costs are spilt between $1.00 per barrel production costs and $1.10 per barrel for converting the crude. The Jose conversion plant is expected to increase the naphtha yield of the crude from 0.5 percent to 9.0 percent, the kerosene/diesel content from 14 to 27 percent, heavy distillates from 28 to 33 percent and reduce the low-value vacuum residue to 31.0 percent from 57.5 percent.
Production of extra-heavy crude is expected to start in 1999, rising to an initial rate of 60,000 barrels per day (bpd), with an eventual target of 120,000 bpd.

About 90,000 bpd of upgraded crude will be shipped to Mobil's Chalmette refinery in Louisiana, in which Lagoven plans to buy a 50 percent stake, and 18,000 bpd is slated for Veba's refineries in Germany.

The document said the companies involved in Orinoco Belt schemes were considering the construction of another pipeline running from Jose, on the north coast, to the Orinoco Belt. This pipeline would be used to transport naphtha, a refined oil product used to dilute the heavy crude for pumping to Jose.
The economics of the scheme were formulated using a marker price of $12.50 per barrel for Mexico's Maya crude, which was the average price over the period 1990-1994.
The project is expected to use a mixture of debt and equity finance, in a 60/40 split, with the debt portion guaranteed by income generated by the project.
